name: Opus 5 dispersion
strategy: Equal-weight 51% long basket of twelve large caps screened for the highest idiosyncratic (residual-to-SPY) volatility and the lowest mutual correlation across eight sectors, hedged with a 47% short of the cap-weighted indices they sit in (28% SPY + 19% QQQ, the split that minimised residual volatility across five half-year windows), leaving 2% cash and roughly zero net index beta.
novelty: The edge hypothesis is dispersion: measured on 101 large caps through the 2026-07-24 close, the average daily cross-sectional standard deviation of returns is 41.5% annualised against SPY's own 13.0% realised vol (a 3.19x ratio) while average pairwise correlation is 0.079 - the 1st percentile of the trailing 2.5 years - so roughly three quarters of a single name's variance is idiosyncratic and the index is an unusually cheap, unusually complete hedge for direction. That makes this a different return driver from long-AI-momentum: the book is beta-hedged (pooled net beta +0.10, currently -0.03), 7 of its 12 longs are outside tech, and its P&L is the scatter of constituents around the index rather than the index's own advance - in the 2026H1 backtest the directional component contributed -0.33% of a +20.25% pre-cost gross return. It is falsified if average pairwise correlation reverts toward its 0.17 two-year mean or spikes on a macro shock, because the basket and the index then move together and only the residual beta mismatch and the 1.4%/yr borrow cost remain; it is also falsified if the basket's idiosyncratic scatter is symmetric, since a linear long/short expression captures the sign of dispersion, not its magnitude.

positions.thesis: Managed care: 52.4% vol with 99% of variance idiosyncratic and a 0.35 measured beta - the purest single-name scatter in the screen, driven by MA rate/utilisation news that has no index analogue.
AI server hardware: 85.5% vol, 81.1% idiosyncratic. Margin-mix outcomes dominate its returns, so it scatters violently around any tech-index move rather than tracking it.
Nitrogen fertiliser: 49.8% vol on a gas/grain spread cycle with essentially no equity-index loading (measured beta -1.4 is noise around zero); a genuine correlation diversifier for the basket.
Memory: 90.5% vol, 78.0% idiosyncratic. Pricing-cycle driven and the single largest scatter contributor among semis, and the QQQ short absorbs the part of it that is just sector beta.
Payments: 49.9% vol with 92% idiosyncratic share and a 0.98 beta - a company-specific re-rating story that is uncorrelated with the rest of the basket (pairwise -0.02 at selection).
Biotech: 71.9% vol, 90% idiosyncratic. Pipeline/readout binaries are the archetypal dispersion asset - large moves that are orthogonal to both SPY and the other eleven names.
Discount retail: 46.4% vol with 96% idiosyncratic share; comp-store and banner-restructuring outcomes, a consumer-side scatter source with no tech overlap.
Enterprise software: 45.9% vol and a measured beta of only 0.23 - 99.5% idiosyncratic. Seat-growth and AI-monetisation debate moves it independently of the software tape.
Mobile/edge semis: 63.4% vol, 76% idiosyncratic, driven by licensing and customer-concentration news rather than the AI capex cycle that dominates QQQ.
Energy: 38.6% vol with a measured beta near zero to slightly negative - the basket's macro-offset leg; crude-driven returns are the classic low-correlation block in a dispersion basket.
Cruise: 53.7% vol, 45.8% idiosyncratic. Booking-curve and capacity news gives it a large company-specific component on top of a cyclical beta the index short already covers.
Government/commercial software: 55.5% vol with 91% idiosyncratic share and a 1.18 beta - high scatter but contract-driven, so it is not a proxy for the AI-hardware complex.

Primary beta hedge. Shorting the cap-weighted index removes market direction while costing little of the basket's risk: hedging cuts basket volatility only from 22.7% to a 7.4% residual, which is the whole point of a 0.08-correlation regime.

Second hedge leg. Five of the twelve longs load on the Nasdaq factor; a 60/40 SPY/QQQ split of the 47% short minimised the book's residual volatility in all five half-year windows tested (6.3-8.8% annualised).

backtest.notes: Engine runs: python3 tracker/round2.py --backtest <entry> <end> on this exact book. A third window, 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30, returned +1.35% with a -5.17% max drawdown against SPY +6.31%. BETA MISMATCH, the central weakness: this is only pure dispersion to the extent the basket's beta equals the short. The equal-weight basket's beta to SPY is 1.02 on the 126-day lookback but 1.22 pooled over 2024-01 to 2026-07 (window range 1.02-1.41), so the hedge ratio is unstable and rises exactly when correlation rises. Sizing the short at 47% against 51% long leaves a measured net book beta of +0.107 (2024H1), +0.145 (2024H2), +0.117 (2025H1), +0.190 (2025H2) and -0.034 (2026H1), pooled +0.102, with book volatility 7.4% annualised and correlation to SPY +0.22 pooled. DECOMPOSITION of pre-cost gross return: 2026H1 +20.25% = -0.33% directional + 20.57% idiosyncratic; 2025H2 +1.50% = +2.76% directional - 1.26% idiosyncratic; 2025H1 +2.02% = +0.78% directional + 1.24% idiosyncratic. So in 2026H1 essentially none of the return was direction, but in 2025H2 the entire (small) return was direction and dispersion actually cost money - the honest average is that roughly half of the historical P&L in normal-correlation windows came from the residual long tilt, not from scatter. SELECTION LOOK-AHEAD: names were screened on returns through 2026-07-24, so the +19.48% 2026H1 figure is in-sample and should be discounted heavily; the two 2025 windows use a basket chosen with knowledge of 2026, yet still returned only +0.87% and +1.35%, which is the more sober estimate of what a stale basket does. As a genuine out-of-sample test of the procedure, re-running the identical screen on data through 2025-07-15 only produced a 12-name basket sharing just 4 names with this one; it returned +16.69% versus SPY +9.87% in 2025H2 and +4.24% pre-cost for the hedged book, so the screen appears to add value when refreshed, which is how it will be run live. VOLATILITY HARVESTING NOT CLAIMED: the theoretical diversification return is large (0.5 x (mean constituent variance 60.9%^2 - basket variance 22.7%^2) = 16.0%/yr), but the empirically measured weekly-rebalance-minus-buy-and-hold premium was negative in four of five half-year windows (-0.05%, -10.32%, +0.89%, -1.95%, -6.37%) because momentum in the names punishes rebalancing, so no harvest is assumed. Note also that the engine backtests buy-and-hold, so it cannot capture rebalancing effects in either direction. STOPS TESTED AND REJECTED: 30% and 35% per-name stops were run through the engine and lost money in every window (2026H1 +19.48% fell to +14.05%/+15.56%, 2025H2 +0.87% fell to -0.06%/+0.87%, 2025H1 +1.35% fell to -0.97%/-0.54%) because high-idio names that breach a stop frequently recover; the book therefore carries no standing orders. COSTS included by the engine: 3% APR borrow on the 47% short (1.41%/yr drag), 4% APY on 2% cash, 2bps per side entry on ~98% gross. Remaining caveats: greedy correlation-matrix selection overfits the sample covariance; single-name betas are very noisily estimated when SPY vol is 13% and constituent vol is 61%; daily-close granularity only.

outlook: I expect a low-volatility, low-beta equity curve - roughly 7-9% annualised book volatility, drawdowns in the 4-6% range, and returns that will look dull against SPY in any strong beta rally and good against SPY in a flat or falling tape. The realistic base case is mid-single-digit annualised excess over cash if the current 1st-percentile correlation regime persists, and roughly flat if it does not. Management: re-run the idiosyncratic-volatility and pairwise-correlation screen every Friday and replace the bottom two or three names rather than holding a stale basket, since the out-of-sample evidence says the refreshed procedure works better than the fixed list; re-estimate the basket's beta weekly and resize the SPY/QQQ short to keep net beta inside +/-0.15, tolerating a small net short rather than a net long given that correlation is far more likely to rise than fall from 0.08. The trade I am watching for is a correlation spike: if the rolling 63-day average pairwise correlation moves back above 0.20, the dispersion premise is gone, the basket and the shorts converge, and I would cut gross exposure toward cash rather than try to ride it out. The dominant risk is a correlated selloff, in which every long falls together, the hedge only offsets its beta share, and the residual +0.10 net long plus the basket's higher-than-index volatility both work against me at once.
